tier_reason: RELEASE_NOTES.md (section 'ChangeLog ongoing', not yet in a tagged release) states vcfputtogetheragain is '~200x faster on large VCFs' than the zig implementation of vcfcreatemulti; that is a first-party one-line claim with no timings, input, hardware, compiler or harness anywhere in the repo (the commit messages and the src/vcfputtogetheragain.c header carry no numbers), so C.

corrections.caveats: Weak entry. The only number is one first-party phrase in the unreleased 'ChangeLog ongoing' section of RELEASE_NOTES.md ('~200x faster on large VCFs'); no timings, input file, hardware, compiler flags or benchmark script exist in the repo, and the speedup is above 50x with no methodology. The baseline is vcflib's own zig code path of vcfcreatemulti, not an incumbent such as bcftools norm -m+, htslib or vcftools, so this is an internal before/after comparison. That zig path crashed with a use-after-free (zig 'index out of bounds' panic) on files with overlapping multi-allelic records until the commit just before vcfputtogetheragain was added, and zig is now disabled by default (NO_ZIG=ON), so the shipped vcfcreatemulti falls back to the legacy C++ implementation, which was not compared. vcfputtogetheragain is a 1:1 C port of the zig logic with documented 'DIFFERENCE' points, and by default it keeps the zig semantics that drop multi-allelic input records (--norm-multiallelic changes this; 256 previously invalid records on the scaffold612 sample), so outputs are not guaranteed identical to the baseline. The 2022 PLoS Comput Biol paper predates this 2026 tool and cannot hold its benchmarks. The vcf-std validation figure (about 0.11 s to 0.04 s) is again self-comparison. Category fit is loose: this is a VCF record-merging transformation tool, not a CSV/tabular parser.

notes: Claim text verified verbatim in RELEASE_NOTES.md; metadata matches (MIT, 686 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-02). Shortcomings: single unmeasured first-party ratio, self baseline (zig path that crashed before a same-week fix and is now off by default), no harness, loose csv-tabular category fit.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Not faster than binpac overall. Reachable harness (evantypanski/spicy-performance README, Feb-Apr 2025, std::clock CPU seconds to parse a 100 MB input, mean of 5 samples, lower is better): BytesUntil Spicy 0.286 s vs binpac 1.635 s (Spicy about 5.7x faster, derived from page data); BytesLength 0.005 vs 0.005 s (equal); Spicy WithUnit 14.087 s vs binpac WithRecord 3.809 s (Spicy about 3.7x slower, derived from page data); WithUnitSwitch 17.232 s vs WithRecordCase 4.128 s (about 4.2x slower, derived from page data); Regex 10.228 s vs binpac 0.378 s (about 27x slower; the README itself says 'Spicy patterns are 27x slower than binpac' and 'Spicy units are also about 3-4x slower'). The 2026-07 'one year later' zeek.org post could not be opened (snippet only): its figures, quoted in snippets as Gbps, fit the seconds scale of this harness (BytesLength is the cheapest test yet shows the smallest value, 0.003 vs 0.002), so they are most likely seconds, which reverses the record's ratios: BytesUntil Spicy 0.268 vs binpac 2.316 (Spicy about 8.6x faster if seconds), WithUnit 9.357 vs 4.663 (Spicy about 2.0x slower), WithUnitSwitch 11.061 vs 4.866 (about 2.3x slower), Regex 4.197 vs 0.000 (binpac value not usable). Spicy 1.16 vs 1.13 end-to-end in Zeek: 1.339 s vs 1.430 s (about 1.07x, version over version, not against binpac).
corrections.workload: Microbenchmarks of generated parsers on one synthetic input (an 8-byte big-endian length followed by 100,000,000 'Z' bytes): Spicy units BytesLength, BytesUntil, Regex, SinkUntil, Sync, SyncRegex, While, WithUnit, WithUnitSwitch versus binpac BytesLength, BytesUntil, WithRecord, WithRecordCase and a Zeek-plugin regex test; the 2026 follow-up post (not opened) reran similar cases inside Zeek 8.2 / Spicy 1.16 and an end-to-end Zeek run across Spicy versions.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: 2025 harness: Spicy side built with spicy-config --cxx and spicy-config --cxxflags --ldflags; binpac side built with a bare 'clang++ ../bench_binpac.cc ... -o binpac-bench' and no -O flag (unoptimized baseline). 2026 post: not known.
corrections.caveats: Spicy is not faster than binpac in general: in both the reachable 2025 harness and the snippet figures of the 2026 zeek.org post, Spicy loses units, unit switches and regex patterns (2x to 27x) and wins only on bytes &until. The 2025 harness's binpac baseline was compiled without any optimization flag ('Just assume the binpac compile command, I don't care enough' in run-benchmark.rb), so even the BytesUntil win is against an -O0 baseline; binpac's Zeek regex dependency was stubbed out, and its regex test needed a patched Compile() call. Timing is std::clock CPU time of a single parse call over one synthetic 100 MB input; no CPU model, compiler version or hardware stated. SNIPPET ONLY for the 2026 post (zeek.org egress-blocked): its numbers are labelled Gbps in search summaries but behave like seconds (BytesLength, the cheapest case, has the smallest value), so the record's 'Spicy about 2.0x/2.3x faster' readings were inverted; units should be confirmed from an environment that can reach zeek.org. The post's own framing (per snippets) is that Spicy stays slower in most real analyzers. Version-over-version gain (Spicy 1.16 vs 1.13, about 1.07x end to end) is not a baseline win.
